newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Boycott of Cairo economic summit widens.
newsitem.headline: Boycott of Cairo economic summit widens.

text.p: Israelis angry at Egypt and Palestinians fuming at Israel said on Monday they would boycott next week's Middle East economic conference in Cairo.

Israel's Agriculture Ministry announced its representatives had stopped their preparations to attend the third annual regional summit because Egyptian chambers of commerce had advised their members to have nothing to do with Israelis.

Palestinian industrialists and business executives said they would not send an official delegation to Cairo in a protest against Israel's economically crippling closures of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
The conference is scheduled to start on November 12.

"The director-general gave the order to people in the ministry who intended to go to Egypt to stop all preparations because Egyptian chambers of commerce said they were ordering their members...to boycott Israel completely," Agriculture Ministry spokesman Naftali Yaniv told Reuters.
Israel's delegation to the conference will be headed by Commerce and Industry Minister Natan Sharansky.

On Sunday, National Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon said no one from his ministry would attend the summit because Egypt's political leaders and newspapers had been attacking the Israeli government.

"All the associations have decided to boycott the Middle East economic conference in Cairo as an expression of protest against Israeli measures which had suffocated our economy and harmed our businesses," said Adnan Faramand, owner of the Arab Food Company and a member of the food manufacturers association.

The Palestinian Authority is expected to attend the conference, which brings together leaders and businessmen from around the world to discuss development projects and cooperation. The meeting follows two similar summits in Amman last year and in Casablanca in Morocco in 1994.

The conferences were originally aimed at integrating Israel into the region's economy. But a faltering peace process since the May election of right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has placed unexpected hurdles before the Cairo gathering.
Many say Israel could find itself ignored by Arab businessmen at the meeting of 85 states. Two months ago, Egypt threatened to cancel the conference if Israel did not make progress in peace talks.

Palestinian business executives said they would meet U.S. Consul-General Edward Abington later on Monday to discuss the Cairo conference. Last month, the U.S. ambassadors to Israel and Egypt spoke to Israeli industrialists and urged them to attend.

Palestinan businessmen said it was imperative for Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's Authority to be at the summit to show support to Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, who has strongly backed the PLO's position in talks with Israel.

Israel imposed a closure earlier this year on the West Bank and Gaza after Islamic militants carried out four suicide bombings in February and March that killed 59 people. The closure has since been eased but tough restrictions remain.
Palestinian businessmen said the closure has increased unemployment in Gaza and the West Bank to over 50 percent and reduced per capita income by 35 percent.
"As a result of the closures, Palestinian goods and people don't have freedom of movement to Israel, but Israel drowns our markets with its goods," Faramand said.
